Lessons.Title: Associations in Categorical Data
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: compare conditional relative frequencies to identify possible association between two categorical variables and distinguish it from causation. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U03:L03, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/3/3/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0); publisher Addressing HSS-ID.B.5. The source uses two-way tables to compare association, not simply raw counts.

Original fictional club preferences: A Sports12 Arts8 (20 total), B Sports9 Arts11 (20 total). Conditional probability-like proportions are P(Sports|A)=.60 and P(Sports|B)=.45, a 15-percentage-point difference suggesting possible association in this invented sample. Nothing about the data proves which group label causes a preference.

Control example with equal group distributions: A Sports12 Arts8, B Sports12 Arts8. Sports proportions in both groups are .60, so this particular table shows no group association with the club preference. Small samples and method of selection limit extrapolation.

Student task: create a labelled pair of side-by-side bar representations and compare row percentages, design a 'no association' table and critique a claim of causation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for accurate conditional frequencies, valid comparison, appropriate no-association example and careful association-versus-causation language.

V13 source-task fidelity: U3L3 requires inspecting a relative-frequency table by the correct conditional population, contrasting one association with nearly matching conditional distributions, and testing associations in other categorical variable pairs. The prior authored club example had only one 15-point contrast and an equal-frequency control, but insufficient cross-context investigation or graph labels.

V13 original fictional aquarium observational sample: 20 tanks have low dissolved-solute levels, with 16 healthy and4 unhealthy; another 20 have high levels, with6 healthy and14 unhealthy. Conditional healthy percentages are 80% and30%. Plot TWO segmented bars with each denominator=20, legend and percentage axes, and explain the 50-percentage-point difference. This suggests a possible association in fictional data only, not chemical causation; other tank variables may confound the relationship.

V13 counterexample and student inquiry: compare an independent 40-response table in which both groups have 10 healthy of20; its conditional rates are equal at50%, indicating no detectable group association in that sample. Then propose two genuinely categorical variables in an ethical, anonymous survey, describe how data would be collected and whether a claim is supported; never invent participants or assert the exercise was administered.

KeyConcepts.Title: Association
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two categorical variables show association when category proportions differ across conditions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare conditional percentages rather than raw totals alone.
KeyConcepts.Example: 60% A versus45% B Sports preferences suggests difference.

KeyConcepts.Title: No detected association
KeyConcepts.Definition: Similar conditional distributions show no evidence of difference in the displayed sample.

KeyConcepts.Title: Correlation does not imply causation
KeyConcepts.Definition: An observed group difference may reflect sampling or omitted variables.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not claim one label changes the other without further design.
KeyConcepts.Example: Group label and preference association does not prove causality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare conditional distributions
WorkedExamples.Question: A Sports12/20 and B Sports9/20.
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.
Steps: Describe a possible association in the fictional sample without causal claim.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A is15 percentage points higher in Sports preference.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both denominators and sample limits stated.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct no-association example
WorkedExamples.Question: Make two groups each20 with the same Sports percent.
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.
Steps: Use A Sports12 and Arts8, total20.
Choose B Sports12 and Arts8, total20.
The displayed conditional distributions match exactly.
WorkedExamples.Answer: In this example, no group difference in Sports proportion.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject unsupported causation
WorkedExamples.Question: Does observing 60% vs45% establish that group membership causes preference?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.
Steps: The table records an association in a fictional sample.
It does not show how membership or preference arose.
Unmeasured selection and chance could affect the distribution.
A causal claim would require additional appropriate design and evidence.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, a table association alone does not establish cause.
WorkedExamples.Check: No experimental assignment or causal proof is shown.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing counts from differently sized rows
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Larger row totals naturally produce more observations.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling a difference proof of causation
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Confounders and selection effects may explain it.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Describe association only unless causal evidence exists.

SummaryPoints: Association is evaluated by comparing conditional distributions.
Equal row proportions are consistent with no group association in the table.
Differences may suggest association without proving cause.
Teacher reviews source limitations and justified claims.
